seoDescription: Learn how to build powerful applications with large language models using Flowise, a no-code visual platform for LangChain. This guide walks you through installing Flowise via node.js and building a custom chatbot from scratch. You'll see how to leverage LangChain components in a drag-and-drop interface, constructing a complete Q&A retrieval system that can answer questions from a PDF document. Discover how to connect document loaders, text splitters, embedding models, and vector stores to create a functional conversational AI.

summary:
## What is Flowise?

Flowise is a **no-code platform** for building applications with **Large Language Models (LLMs)**. It provides a drag-and-drop graphical user interface to visually assemble components from the **LangChain** library. It is built on **Node.js** and is functionally similar to another popular tool, LangFlow.

## Installation & Setup

1.  **Prerequisite**: You must have **Node.js** installed on your system. You can verify the installation by running `npm` in your terminal.
2.  **Install Flowise**: Run the global install command: `npm install -g flowise`
3.  **Start the Server**: Launch the Flowise server with: `npx flowwise start`
4.  **Access the UI**: Open your web browser and navigate to `http://localhost:3000`.

## Building a Document Q&A Bot

The video demonstrates how to build a **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** chatbot that can answer questions based on an uploaded PDF file.

### Core Components & Flow

-   **Document Loader**: Use the `PDF File` loader node to upload your source document (e.g., the US Constitution).
-   **Text Splitter**: Connect a `Recursive Character Text Splitter` to break the document into smaller, manageable chunks.
-   **Embeddings**: Add an `OpenAI Embeddings` node to convert the text chunks into numerical vectors.
-   **Vector Store**: Use an `In-Memory Vector Store` to hold the document chunks and their corresponding embeddings. This node takes the splitter and the embedding model as inputs.
-   **QA Chain**: Add the `Conversational Retrieval QA` chain. This is the core logic unit.
-   **Language Model**: Connect an `OpenAI` LLM node (e.g., `text-davinci-003`) to the QA chain to generate answers.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> To use OpenAI's models for embeddings and generation, you must provide your **OpenAI API Key** in the credentials section of the respective nodes.

## Key Takeaways

-   **Deployment**: Flowise makes it easy to deploy your chatbot. The "Use API" feature provides code snippets for embedding in **HTML**, calling from a **Python** script, or using the **CLI**.
-   **Marketplace**: Flowise includes a marketplace with pre-built templates for popular agent frameworks like **Auto-GPT** and **BabyAGI**, which you can use to start new projects.
-   **Model Behavior**: The chosen LLM (e.g., `text-davinci-003`) may use its pre-existing knowledge in addition to the context from your document. To limit responses to **only** the provided document, you will need to implement specific **prompt engineering** techniques.

> [!TIP]
> If the chat interface appears grayed out and is unusable after saving a flow, try stopping the server (`Ctrl+C` in the terminal) and restarting it with `npx flowwise start`.
transcription:
## Introducing Flowise: A No-Code LangChain Platform

Today we're going to be looking at yet another amazing project called Flowise. It's a no-code platform that lets you build powerful applications using large language models. Flowise is very similar to another great project called LangFlow when it comes to functionality and the interface. I already made a video on LangFlow, so the link is going to be in the description of the video. Check that out if you are interested.

Flowise is written in Node.js. Now, it essentially gives you a graphical user interface where you can use components from LangChain to build applications based on large language models. So for example, there is a simple LLM chain, or you can develop apps for Q&A retrieval. Now there are example applications that you can build for translation, and you can even use conversational agents with memory from LangChain.

In this video, I'm going to show you how to install it on your local machine, and then we will build a couple of applications, including one for Q&A retrieval. We will provide a PDF file and then use Flowise to create a chain for information retrieval.

If you don't mind coding and want to run everything locally without anything leaving your computer, then check on my project called Local GPT. The project is already trending on GitHub, and I'm planning to add a whole bunch of features with the support from the community. So check that out, link is going to be in the description.

## Installing Flowise with Node.js

Okay, coming back to Flowise, let's walk through the installation process. So they have a pretty nice GitHub repo, as always, has around 7,000 stars on GitHub. Okay, so at first let's look at the UI. This is how the UI is going to look like. So it's a simple drag-and-drop interface.

Now, in order to install Flowise, you will need to install Node.js. So using this link, go to the Node.js website and depending on your operating system, you need to install it. So I have already installed it and I am using a Windows machine. So in order to test it, you can simply type in `npm` and just click enter. And if it's installed properly, you will see something like this. 

Okay, so for simple installation, I'm going to be following the exact instructions here. So I already have Node.js installed. So I'm going to type in `npm install -g flowwise`. So that's `flowwise`, click enter, and let's wait for the installation to complete. 

Okay, so the installation is complete. Now, if you want to start Flowise, you can do it in two ways. You can simply type in `npx flowwise start` or you can use `npx flowwise start` and then give it a username and password. This is going to be good if you want to authenticate your users, and that way you provide them a password and whenever you run the Flowise app, they will have to provide that. But in my case, I'm going to simply type in the first option, so that's going to be `npx flowwise` and then we will just start it.

Okay, so once you start it and then if you see this message, "Data source has been initiated and Flowise service is listening at 3000 port number." Right now, you actually need to type in or go to the localhost with the port 3000. I would personally like for them to actually put this here because if you're new to it, you might run this and then you don't know what is actually happening.

## Exploring the Flowise Interface & Marketplace

Now in order to access the server, simply copy this address and then paste it in your browser and just access it. Okay, so I have been playing around with it. I created a couple of apps, we will go with this. But the first thing that I'm going to do, I'm going to switch to dark theme.

So let's look at a few components. First, there is Chatflows. So every flow that you create, it's going to be here. I've been testing with it, so I have a test flow and PDF flow. We will look at this specific rule in a little bit. 

So then there is this marketplace where people have created their pre-built flows that you can use as a template. So for example, here's a flow for Auto-GPT, and then there is this one for Baby AGI, right? And there is even some, for example, if you want to really automate your things, right? 

So if you want to use them as a template, simply click on it and then click on "Use Template" and it brings that flow into your new flow or they are calling it Chatflow. So you can give it a name and then start using it. But we're going to first look at how you can create one from scratch. So for that, simply go to this "Add New" and it will give you a completely blank screen.

## Overview of Available LangChain Components

This is going to be an introductory video where we will look at different components that are available inside Flowise. I will be creating more detailed videos if there is interest.

In order to see which components or modules are available, so click on this plus node. Then it gives you all the available things. So it has a bunch of agents that you can use. You can create different type of chains, and this is actually a pretty comprehensive list. Now keep in mind, this gets inspiration from LangChain. Now if you don't know what LangChain is, I would recommend check out this video.

So in terms of chat models, they have Azure Chat, OpenAI, then even they have an Anthropic, and it supports local chat models as well. For example, LLaMA-CPP or GPT-4-All. So this is pretty neat.

And then there are document loaders so you can load different types of files. Now in terms of embeddings, it has support for OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Cohere, Hugging Face and OpenAI. And it also supports different types of LLMs, so it's pretty similar to what is available inside LangChain. Then different types of memories, and I think it does have a prompt template, so that's pretty neat. There are some retrievers and text splitters. So we are going to be using this recursive text splitter in our example. So this is pretty awesome. And different types of vector stores.

## Understanding the Q&A Retrieval Architecture

In this video, we are going to be building a document question and answer LLM. If you're a regular viewer of my channel, you probably have seen this diagram. So essentially, we're going to upload PDF files, then it will divide it into different sub-documents, we'll compute embeddings for each subdocument, and we'll create a vector store. 

And then whenever a new query or question comes in, we will compute the embeddings using the same embedding models that we used for our vector store, do a semantic search on the vector store to retrieve the most relevant documents or chunks that are inside the knowledge base or vector store, and then rank those results, give those back to a generative large language model, and the user will get a response.

If you are new to these concepts, I would highly recommend you check out this video, which goes in extreme details and explains each one of these components.

## Building the Flow: Data Ingestion Pipeline

Okay, the information that we are going to be providing is going to be in the form of a PDF. So we need a PDF document loader first. So simply go to Document Loaders and check out where PDF Loader is. So you can simply drag it here. I'm going to zoom out a little bit so that we can see everything. In this case, it lets you upload a file. Now, if you simply click on it, then it will take you to your computer and you can upload your file. In this case, we're going to be uploading the Constitution of the United States. 

Now, it expects one input, right? And there is one output. The input that it expects is a text splitter. So we need to provide a text splitter using which we will divide our PDF file into smaller chunks or documents. Okay, so for that, we will just go back again, and then we will look at Text Splitters. Now, in this case, I'm going to be using the Recursive Character Splitter. Now, in order to connect this as an input, simply drag it here, and now you have your text splitter. 

Now, in terms of the overall architecture diagram, so here we are, we are simply dividing or splitting our document into different chunks. Now, by default, the size of each chunk is around 1,000 tokens, and I usually like to put an overlap. 

So next, we need to add two components. One is going to be the embedding computation part, and the second is going to be the vector store. So let's add the embeddings part. For simplicity, we're going to be simply using OpenAI's embeddings, but later on in the subsequent videos, I will show you how you can connect other types of embeddings, for example, embeddings from Hugging Face, which are open source and free to use. 

Now next, we need to take these documents as well as the embeddings and put them together in a vector store so that we can start computing embeddings. The way you do it is we're going to be using a vector store. So let's go to the vector store portion. And here are different options. So you can use ChromaDB, In-Memory Vector Store, Pinecone as well, and then there is Weaviate and a couple of other options. For this simple example, I'm going to be using In-Memory Vector Store. 

So I know in this case we simply need to connect the chunks of documents that we created, and the embedding model. So this is the OpenAI's embeddings model, and the output is going to be the memory retriever. So, here again, we created a knowledge base.

## Building the Flow: The Conversational QA Chain

Now we need to take care of the second component, which is the actual information retrieval part, when somebody asks a question. So for that, we are going to be creating a conversational retrieval question and answer chain. So I'm going to go to the Chains part, all right, and then we will look at this Conversational Retrieval Question and Answer, document QA chain. So let's bring it here.

Now it expects two inputs, one is the language model and the second one is the vector store retriever. So the vector store retriever is coming in from here, and now we need to add a language model. And that's the language model over here. Actually, I have represented it twice so I'm going to just remove that, and so this is how it's going to look like. We'll get the results and now we need a language model in our chain, or actually in our Chatflow. 

So let's simply go here and look at different LLMs that are in here. So for this simple example, I'm going to be using the OpenAI and the LangChain. So I'm going to bring it here and then we need to connect it. That's it.

Now in terms of the different models, I don't think it supports ChatGPT or GPT-4 right now. I might be wrong, but here are the options that you see. Now there are some additional parameters as well. For example, the max token, top probability, batch size, timeout, and things like that, you can adjust those parameters. Similarly for the OpenAI embedding models, there are some additional parameters. Or you can even look at the PDF file reader right? So there are different options that you can set. In this simple example, we're not going to change anything, but we'll keep everything to the default.

## Configuration, Deployment, and Troubleshooting

Okay, now since we're using OpenAI's models, both for embedding as well as for the LLM, so we need to provide an OpenAI API key. Okay, so I copied my API key, I'm going to paste it here and also here. And then what you need to do is you need to simply go and save your Chatflow. So, let's call it Doc_Chat. Okay, and I'm going to just save this.

Okay, once you save it, you will see this code sign. Now this gives you a few options. For example, if you want to embed this into an HTML file, so all you need to do is simply copy this HTML and add it in your HTML file and you'll have a chatbot. Similarly, you can use this in API calls. So for example, here is the API URL if you're doing it in Python. Now notice that it's using your localhost, right? So in order to deploy it in production, you probably want to host it somewhere else. Right? But this is how you're going to make a query. We're going to be looking at this in another video. Okay, then there's a simple sample code to do this exactly in JavaScript as well or if you want to do it through command line. 

Now in terms of other options, you can duplicate your Chatflow. Or if you have already exported the Chatflow, you can load it as well. If you export this Chatflow, it will simply create a JSON file which has all this information listed in there. 

Now, once you create your flow, then click on save. You probably will have to wait a little bit, but then you can click on this chat side and you can type in your question and start chatting with your documents. Now, sometimes when you click on this, you will see that this is grayed out and you're not able to chat with the bot, right? In that case, I would actually recommend you to simply go to the terminal, right, enter control C. So it will stop your web server, and start it again, right? And go to that same process again. That seems to help.

## Testing the Document Q&A Bot

Okay, we can start chatting with the document. So let me ask it a couple of simple questions. So the first question that I'm going to ask is, "What is the term limit for the president?" and let's see what it comes up with. So here's what it came up with. So, "No person should be elected to the office of the president more than twice and no person who has held the office of the president or acted as the president for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected president shall be elected to the office of the President more than once." Okay, this is a very interesting answer, but let's see if we can actually find this in the original Constitution. Okay, so it seems like it actually simply got the answer from here and returned the whole small paragraph. That is interesting. 

All right. And next I asked it, "According to the text of the document, how many states are in the United States?" Since the last amendment is based on 1992, so it actually came up with the correct answer of 50 states. 

Now another question I asked was, "What is the role of the Congress in Congress?" and it kind of came up with this answer. Now, one thing to realize, we're using text-davinci-003 as the LLM. That means it actually has access to the current information as well. Now in order to simply extract information from the document, we will need to do some prompt engineering. In the subsequent videos, I will show you how you can design prompts so that you force the model to extract information only from the documents that you provide.

## Conclusion and Final Thoughts

Overall, Flowise, just like LangFlow, is a great no-code tool that lets you build powerful applications based on large language models. I would recommend everybody to actually check both of them out if you are looking to build your own applications based on large language models and want to figure out the feasibility.

I do provide consulting services. For consulting, check out the description of the video for further details or the pinned comment. We also have a Discord server, which is actually growing, and there are some awesome people who are helping each other out with different projects. I would recommend everybody to check it out if you are looking for a community of like-minded people.

If you like what you see on this channel and would like to support it, you can check out a couple of links in the description of the video on how to do that. As always, thanks for watching and see you in the next one.
